title: Basic Types
summary: TypeScript's **primitive and special types** — `string`, `number`, `boolean`, arrays, `object`, `null`/`undefined`, and the special `any`, `unknown`, `void`, and `never` — are the vocabulary you use to describe what your values *are*, so the compiler can check how they're used.

subtopics.title: Primitives: string, number, boolean
subtopics.explanation: These three cover the everyday data of most programs. They are written in lowercase (string, not String) and correspond exactly to JavaScript's primitive types. number covers integers and floats alike; there is no separate int type.

subtopics.title: Arrays: T[] and Array<T>
subtopics.explanation: An array type says what kind of elements it holds. There are two equivalent syntaxes: number[] and Array<number>. Use whichever your team prefers; the bracket form is more common for simple element types.
subtopics.example:
let scores: number[] = [90, 85];
let names: Array<string> = ['a', 'b'];

subtopics.title: The object type
subtopics.explanation: object means 'any non-primitive value' — it's rarely what you want, because it allows any object shape and exposes no specific properties. Usually you describe the exact shape with an object literal type or interface instead.
subtopics.example:
let config: object = { debug: true }; // works, but config.debug is an error
let point: { x: number; y: number } = { x: 1, y: 2 }; // better

subtopics.title: null and undefined
subtopics.explanation: These are TypeScript types as well as JavaScript values. Under strictNullChecks, they are not assignable to other types unless you explicitly include them (string | null), which forces you to handle the 'missing' case and prevents the classic 'cannot read property of undefined' crash.
subtopics.example:
let nickname: string | null = null;
let middle: string | undefined; // undefined by default

subtopics.title: any: the escape hatch
subtopics.explanation: any turns off type checking for a value — you can do anything to it and the compiler won't complain. It's useful for gradual migration but dangerous: it silently spreads and disables the safety TypeScript is meant to provide. Avoid it when you can.
subtopics.example:
let data: any = JSON.parse(input);
data.foo.bar(); // no error, even if it crashes at runtime

subtopics.title: unknown: the safe any
subtopics.explanation: unknown is the type-safe counterpart to any. You can assign anything to an unknown, but you cannot use it until you narrow it (with typeof, a check, or a cast). It says 'I don't know the type yet, so prove what it is before using it.'
subtopics.example:
let value: unknown = JSON.parse(input);
if (typeof value === 'string') value.toUpperCase(); // safe

subtopics.title: void and never
subtopics.explanation: void is the return type of functions that don't return a useful value (they return undefined). never is the type of values that can't occur — used for functions that always throw or never finish, and for exhaustiveness checks. void = 'returns nothing useful'; never = 'never returns at all'.
subtopics.example:
function log(msg: string): void { console.log(msg); }
function fail(m: string): never { throw new Error(m); }

subtopics.title: Type space vs value space
subtopics.explanation: TypeScript has two parallel worlds: types (which exist only at compile time) and values (which exist at runtime). A name can mean different things in each. typeof has two roles too: the JavaScript operator that returns a string at runtime, and the TypeScript operator that reads a value's type at compile time.

foundations.overview: Basic types are the building blocks of every TypeScript annotation. They let you describe the kind of data a variable, parameter, or return value holds, so the compiler can verify that you only use it in compatible ways. Mastering the primitives plus the special types (any, unknown, void, never) and understanding null-handling is the foundation everything else — interfaces, generics, unions — builds on.
foundations.formalDefinition: TypeScript's basic types include the primitive types (string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol), structural types (arrays and objects), the nullable types (null, undefined), and the special top/bottom and utility types: any (opt-out of checking), unknown (the safe top type), void (no useful return), and never (the empty bottom type).
foundations.whyItMatters: You can't type anything without these. Choosing the right basic type — especially unknown over any, and modeling null explicitly — is the difference between code TypeScript actually protects and code where the type system is silently disabled. Interviewers probe these distinctions (any vs unknown, void vs never) to test real understanding.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of types as labels on boxes describing what's inside. Primitives label simple contents; arrays label 'a box of these'; any is an unlabeled box you promise not to check; unknown is a sealed box you must open and inspect before use; never is a box that can never be filled.
foundations.browserPerspective: All of these types are erased at compile time. At runtime there is only JavaScript, where typeof reports the actual primitive kind ('string', 'number', 'object'). The TypeScript types guided the compiler; the running browser only sees plain values.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Every typed variable, function parameter, and API model uses these. unknown is common for JSON.parse results and caught errors; void for event handlers and callbacks; union with null/undefined for optional data; never for exhaustive switch checks.
foundations.businessImpact: Modeling null/undefined explicitly eliminates a leading cause of production crashes (null-reference errors), and avoiding any keeps the type system's bug-catching value intact — directly reducing incidents.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Precise basic types give accurate autocomplete and catch misuse at the boundary. Reaching for any erodes safety across the codebase, while unknown forces explicit, reviewable handling of uncertain data.
foundations.performanceImpact: None at runtime — all type information is erased. The choices affect correctness and developer experience, not execution speed.
commonUseCases: Typing variables and function parameters with primitives
Modeling optional/missing data with string | null or string | undefined
Using unknown for JSON.parse output and caught errors, then narrowing
Using never for exhaustiveness checks in switch statements

commonMisconceptions.myth: any and unknown are basically the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: any disables checking entirely; unknown stays type-safe by forcing you to narrow it before use. Prefer unknown.

commonMisconceptions.myth: void and never mean the same 'nothing'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: void means the function returns (with no useful value); never means it never returns at all — it throws or loops forever.

visualExplorer.title: Choosing the right type for a value
visualExplorer.caption: A decision path from a raw value to the most precise basic type.

config.intro: Walk through picking a type as data flows from input to use.

steps.name: Is it a simple value?
steps.detail: Text -> string, a quantity -> number, a flag -> boolean. Use the lowercase primitive.

steps.name: Is it a list?
steps.detail: A collection of one element type becomes T[] or Array<T>, e.g. number[].

steps.name: Could it be missing?
steps.detail: If it may be absent, model it explicitly with | null or | undefined so you handle the empty case.

steps.name: Is the type unknown right now?
steps.detail: For JSON.parse or caught errors, use unknown — not any — so you must check before using it.

steps.name: Narrow before use
steps.detail: Use typeof or a check to refine unknown to a concrete type, then operate on it safely.

steps.name: Avoid any
steps.detail: Reach for any only as a last-resort escape hatch; it silently disables checking and spreads.

interactiveExamples.title: Primitives and arrays at runtime
interactiveExamples.explanation: The annotations are erased; typeof reports the underlying JavaScript primitive. Arrays are just JS arrays.

interactiveExamples.title: unknown forces you to narrow
interactiveExamples.explanation: An unknown value can't be used directly. typeof narrows it to a concrete type before use — the safe alternative to any.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: text of length 5 / number worth 42 / something else

codeLab.title: Type a value-describing function with unknown
codeLab.instructions: Type the parameter as unknown and narrow it so the function returns 'even', 'odd', or 'not a number'. Keep it type-safe — don't use any. describe(4) should log 'even'.
hints: Guard with typeof value !== 'number' first, then it's safe to treat value as a number.

debuggingLab.title: any silently hides a bug
debuggingLab.symptom: Code that should be type-checked compiles fine but crashes or produces nonsense at runtime.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Typing response as any turns off all checking, so accessing the misspelled response.usr is allowed at compile time. At runtime response.usr is undefined, and reading .name on undefined throws. unknown would have forced a check first.
commonMistakes: Reaching for any to quickly silence a type error.
Trusting parsed/external data without narrowing it from unknown.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Replace any with a precise type (or unknown plus narrowing) so the typo is caught and access is safe.

theory.question: What is the difference between any and unknown?
theory.directAnswer: Both can hold a value of any type, but any disables type checking — you can do anything to it with no error — while unknown stays type-safe: you can assign anything to it, but you must narrow it (with typeof, a check, or a cast) before you can use it. Prefer unknown so the compiler still protects you.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: any is the opt-out-of-checking type; unknown is the safe top type that accepts anything but permits nothing until narrowed.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: any supports gradual migration and interop; unknown gives a safe way to represent 'type not known yet' without disabling checking.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Operations on any are always allowed; operations on unknown are errors until you narrow it to a specific type.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing unknown over any is a core best practice; this question tests whether you understand how to keep code type-safe when dealing with uncertain data.
theory.realWorldExample: JSON.parse returns any by default; assigning its result to unknown forces you to validate the shape before trusting it.

nestedTopics.title: Narrowing
nestedTopics.explanation: Using typeof/checks to refine unknown to a usable type.

nestedTopics.title: Why any spreads
nestedTopics.explanation: Values derived from any are also any, silently disabling checks downstream.

nestedTopics.title: Top types
nestedTopics.explanation: Both are 'top' types that accept any value, but only unknown stays safe.

followUps.question: When is using any actually acceptable?
followUps.answer: As a temporary escape hatch during migration or quick prototyping, or at genuinely untyped boundaries — but it should be isolated and replaced with precise types or unknown as soon as possible.

followUps.question: How do you turn an unknown into a usable type?
followUps.answer: Narrow it with typeof, instanceof, property checks, or a runtime validator (like Zod); only then can you safely use it.

theory.question: What is the difference between void and never?
theory.directAnswer: void is the return type of a function that completes but returns no useful value (it returns undefined) — like a logger. never is the return type of a function that never returns at all, because it always throws or loops forever. void means 'returns nothing meaningful'; never means 'never reaches a return'.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: void describes the absence of a useful return value; never describes the absence of any value because the function cannot complete normally.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: void models side-effect functions and callbacks; never models impossible states and powers exhaustiveness checks.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A void function ends normally with undefined; a never function exits abnormally (throw) or never exits, so control never returns to the caller.

theory.whyImportant: It's a classic distinction interviewers use to test depth; never also underpins exhaustive switch handling, a common real-world pattern.
theory.realWorldExample: function fail(msg: string): never { throw new Error(msg); } can be called in a switch's default to force handling of every case.

nestedTopics.title: Exhaustiveness checks
nestedTopics.explanation: Assigning a value to a never parameter in a switch default catches unhandled cases at compile time.

nestedTopics.title: void in callbacks
nestedTopics.explanation: void return types let callbacks return something that's simply ignored.

nestedTopics.title: Bottom type
nestedTopics.explanation: never is assignable to every type but nothing is assignable to it.

followUps.question: Why is never useful in a switch statement?
followUps.answer: If you assign the switched value to a never-typed variable in the default case, adding a new unhandled variant becomes a compile error — guaranteeing you handle every case.

scenario.question: You're consuming an external API and someone typed the parsed response as any, causing typos and missing-field bugs to slip through. How do you make it safe?
scenario.directAnswer: Stop using any at the boundary. Type the parsed result as unknown and narrow it, or define an explicit interface for the expected shape and validate the incoming data at runtime (e.g. with Zod) before trusting it. This restores compile-time checking so typos and missing fields are caught.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Replacing an any boundary with unknown plus narrowing, or a typed-and-validated shape.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: any erases the type at the boundary, defeating TypeScript's purpose right where data is least trustworthy.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: unknown forces explicit checks; a runtime validator both checks the data and returns a precisely typed value.

scenario.whyImportant: API boundaries are where untyped data enters; handling them safely is a frequent real-world and interview concern.

nestedTopics.title: unknown at boundaries
nestedTopics.explanation: Use unknown for data you don't yet trust, then narrow.

nestedTopics.title: Runtime validation
nestedTopics.explanation: Types can't check runtime data; validators bridge that gap and return typed values.

nestedTopics.title: Why any is risky here
nestedTopics.explanation: It silently allows typos and wrong-field access at the riskiest point in the app.

followUps.question: Why can't TypeScript just verify the API response matches the interface?
followUps.answer: Types are erased at compile time and the response only exists at runtime, so TypeScript can't check it on its own — you need an actual runtime validation step.

coding.question: Write a type-safe function safeLength that accepts an unknown value and returns its length if it's a string or array, otherwise 0.
coding.thoughtProcess: The input is uncertain, so I type it as unknown — never any. I narrow with typeof for string and Array.isArray for arrays; both have a .length property once narrowed. Anything else returns 0. The narrowing is what makes accessing .length safe and type-checked.
coding.lineByLine: value: unknown accepts anything but allows nothing until narrowed. typeof value === 'string' narrows to string, so value.length is valid. Array.isArray(value) narrows to an array, also exposing .length. The final return 0 handles every other type. unknown forces these guards, keeping the code safe.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) — type checks and a property read.

alternativeApproaches.title: Using any (unsafe)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Typing the parameter as any would compile but allow value.length on numbers, returning undefined and defeating the safety.
alternativeApproaches.code: // function safeLength(value: any): number { return value.length ?? 0; } // unsafe

followUps.question: Why use unknown instead of any for the parameter?
followUps.answer: unknown forces the typeof and Array.isArray guards before accessing .length, so the compiler guarantees you only read .length on values that actually have it.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Basic types form the leaves of every type in the system — interfaces, unions, and generics are all composed from them. Teams establish conventions (prefer unknown over any, model null explicitly, avoid object) so the type vocabulary stays consistent across the codebase.
productionDeepDive.performance: No runtime impact; all type information is erased. The practical cost is purely about correctness and developer experience — precise types catch more bugs and give better autocomplete.
productionDeepDive.security: Using unknown at trust boundaries (API responses, user input, JSON.parse) instead of any forces validation before use, reducing the risk of acting on malformed or malicious data. Types alone don't validate, so they're paired with runtime checks.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As a codebase grows, banning implicit any (noImplicitAny) and disallowing explicit any via lint rules keeps type coverage from silently eroding. Modeling null/undefined explicitly under strictNullChecks prevents a whole class of crashes at scale.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Precise basic types document intent and make refactors safe. Overusing any or object hides information and pushes bugs to runtime, so reviews typically flag them.
productionDeepDive.observability: tsc --noEmit in CI catches misuse of types before deploy. Lint rules like no-explicit-any surface where the type system has been bypassed so it can be addressed.

caseStudies.problem: Frequent 'cannot read property of undefined' crashes in production from values that could be null.
caseStudies.solution: Enabled strictNullChecks so null/undefined must be modeled explicitly and handled before use.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More upfront annotations and null-handling in exchange for eliminating a leading crash category.
caseStudies.lessons: Modeling absence explicitly with the type system removes bugs that dynamic typing lets slip to runtime.

projectBuilder.summary: Define the core data types for the Expense Tracker using basic types, and safely parse incoming data with unknown.
requirements: An Expense shape using primitives and arrays
A safe parse helper that takes unknown and narrows it
projectBuilder.architecture: A types module declares Expense with string/number/boolean fields and an optional note. A parse module accepts unknown JSON and validates it into a typed Expense before the rest of the app uses it.

steps.title: Define the Expense type
steps.instructions: Create type Expense = { id: string; amount: number; settled: boolean; note: string | undefined }.
steps.checkpoint: Fields autocomplete with correct types when used.

steps.title: Model arrays
steps.instructions: Type the store as Expense[] and add a couple of entries.
steps.checkpoint: Pushing a wrong-shaped object is a compile error.

steps.title: Safely parse input
steps.instructions: Write parseExpense(input: unknown): Expense | null that narrows before returning.
steps.checkpoint: Invalid input returns null instead of crashing.

enhancements: Add a never-based exhaustiveness check over an expense category union
Replace manual narrowing with a Zod schema returning Expense
interviewQuestions: Why type the parse input as unknown instead of any?
How would you model an optional field, and what does strictNullChecks change?

keyTakeaways: Primitives (string, number, boolean), arrays (T[] / Array<T>), and the object type describe everyday data.
Model missing values explicitly with null/undefined; under strictNullChecks this prevents many runtime crashes.
Prefer unknown over any: unknown stays type-safe by forcing you to narrow before use, while any disables checking.
void means a function returns nothing useful; never means it never returns (throws or loops forever).
Types live in a separate compile-time 'type space' from runtime values and are erased before the code runs.
